catalog_citation: Krahmalkov, Charles R. 2001. A Phoenician-Punic Grammar (Handbook of Oriental Studies 54). Leiden: Brill.
catalog_locator: Ch. II 'The Alphabet, Orthography and Phonology', sec. 4 'Word-Stress and Vowel Reduction', p. 33 (archive.org djvu text); cf. sec. 4c p. 36 an…
catalog_quote: Word-stress was, as in Hebrew, on final syllable in most instances. This word-final stress was already characteristic of Phoenician in the Assyrian period, as seen in numerous transcriptions of Phoenician personal and place names in which the word-final stress is indicated by gemination of the final consonant: Tig. Pil. III 67.66 Tyre Me-te-en-na Mettén (personal name); Esar. ii 65 Sidon Ma-'-ru-ub-bu Ma‘réb (place-name) ... As in other West Semitic languages; vowel reduction in Phoenician was related to word-stress. Word-stress and vowel reduction in Phoenician were essentially identical to Hebrew: full reduction to zero or partial reduction, with resultant shewa.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and the exception passages are verbatim in the held Krahmalkov 2001 djvu text at the stated section and page (p. 33, sec. II.4; pronoun passages pp. 39-40). (2) Deciding source: a 2001 Brill reference grammar with a dedicated word-stress section — for an extinct, consonantally written language this is the best kind of source that can exist; the only peer (PPG3 1999) is not open. (3) downloaded now: Harris 1936 (open archive.org scan), sec. 8 pp. 25-26, independently states final stress with penultimate stress where an old long final vowel survived, 'as in Hebrew' — confirms the classification (final stress, lexically identified penultimate minority). (4) No database contradictions in the record; nothing suggests a reclassify.

sources.citation: Harris, Zellig S. 1936. A Grammar of the Phoenician Language (American Oriental Series 8). New Haven: American Oriental Society. [archive.org open Princeton scan, id grammarofphoenic00harr, djvu text]
sources.quote: 'Phoenician appears to have had a strong stress accent, usually on the final syllable of the word (final after the dropping of final short vowels). ... The place of the accent, and its strong stress character, may be judged from the apparent reduction of short unaccented vowels in the first syllable ... Where the final vowel was long, as in certain verbal forms, the penult position of the accent is still seen, as in Hebrew: nasot for *naxott ... These correspondences show that we have in Phoenician the same accent shift which took place in Canaanite and which is seen in Hebrew.'

sources.citation: Briquel Chatonnet, Françoise & Robert Hawley. 2020. Phoenician and Punic. In Rebecca Hasselbach-Andee (ed.), A Companion to Ancient Near Eastern Languages (Blackwell Companions to the Ancient World), 297-318. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley Blackwell. [author accepted manuscript: HAL hal-03097955]
sources.note: The 'Phoenician phonology' section has only 'Consonants' and 'Vowels' (AM pp. 11-14); there is no stress/accent subsection and no statement on tone or pitch anywhere in the chapter; stress is only alluded to as a conditioning environment for vowel allophony ('in certain syllabic or stress-related environments'; short /i/ lowered 'in at least some syllabic or stress environments'). An independent recent sketch that, like all others, treats Phoenician prosody as (unstated) word stress only.

tone.quote: Some etymological short vowels seem to have developed conditioned allophones in certain syllabic or stress-related environments.

sources.citation: Gzella, Holger. 2011. Phoenician. In Holger Gzella (ed.), Languages from the World of the Bible, 55-75. Boston/Berlin: De Gruyter.
sources.note: The phonology section (pp. 57-59) covers the 22-consonant inventory and its mergers, the short/long vowel system, monophthongization, the Canaanite and Phoenician shifts and Punic vowel reduction; prosody enters only as word stress ('tonic syllable', stress-conditioned /a/ > [o], final stress on nouns after loss of case vowels). Nothing is said about tone, pitch or intonation; the string 'tone' occurs in the chapter only inside 'stone'.
